title: The Story of the Bible: A Study of the Whole Canon
subtitle: A five-session study on the Bible as a single story, from creation to new creation.
summary:
This study is for anyone who has read the Bible in pieces and suspected it was meant to be read whole: skeptics who dismissed it as a grab bag of ancient rules and comforting verses, Christians who know the parts but have never seen the shape, and the small groups that hold both. Over five sessions it follows one story from its first line to its last: creation and the world made good, the fall and the long unraveling, Israel and the promise God kept through a covenant people, Christ and the turning of the whole thing, and new creation, heaven come down to a healed earth. It draws on N. T. Wright's picture of the Bible as a drama in acts and on the older frame of creation, fall, redemption and restoration, because the Bible tells itself that way. A volunteer can lead it with little preparation. Every question comes with notes on what's behind it, and every session ends in prayer.

The study doesn't stand above the Bible and grade it. Many people, skeptics and believers alike, read Scripture as fragments: a verse for weddings, a verse for funerals, a verse for whatever you already wanted to do. The skeptic is right that fragments cut loose can be made to say almost anything. The study's claim is that fragments aren't all there is. The sixty-six books form one unfolding story, with a beginning that explains the ache, an ending that answers it, and a cross at the center. Read that way, the Bible stops being a rulebook to obey or reject and becomes a story you may find yourself inside. Then the question is no longer whether the verses are useful. It's whether the story is true.
audience: Skeptics, new believers, longtime Christians, and small groups

sessions.title: Creation, and the World That Was Good
sessions.aim: To read Genesis 1 and 2 as the opening act of the whole story rather than a science manual to defend or dismiss: a world spoken good by God and a human made in his image for a life of shalom, so that everything the Bible says afterward is measured against what was lost here.
sessions.summary:
The quickest way to misread the whole Bible is to start it on the wrong page. Many of us start at the fall, as if the human condition were the baseline and grace a ladder out of a hole we were always in. But the story doesn't begin in a hole. It begins in a garden, with a God who makes things and calls them good, six times, and then over all of it "very good."

The fight everyone wants to have is about how the world was made. Genesis is asking something else: what the world is. Its answer is that reality isn't an accident or a machine but a gift, and that the human isn't a clever animal but an image bearer, given work, a companion and a garden to keep.

The modern account, that the universe is matter and energy and meaning is something we project, deserves a fair hearing. It's rigorous, and it has explained a great deal. But it can't stop assuming what it denies, that a sunset is beautiful and cruelty is wrong. The Bible's word for the world as it was meant to be is shalom: everything in its right place. Every page after this is either the loss of it or the long work of getting it back.

keyScripture.why: "And God saw everything that he had made, and behold, it was very good" (Genesis 1:31). The world isn't neutral raw material or a ruin from the start. It's a gift its Maker called good, and the rest of the story is measured against it.

discussion.q: When you think of where the Bible's story starts, do you think first of creation or of the fall? What changes if it begins with a world called good?
discussion.behind: Reset the starting line. Many Christians carry a gospel that begins with sin, so grace becomes rescue from a default hole. But Scripture begins with a garden, which means brokenness is the intruder and goodness came first. Let the goodness land before anyone brings up the fall.

discussion.q: Read Genesis 1:26-28. What do you think it means that human beings are made "in the image of God"? What would it change about how you see the person next to you?
discussion.behind: Don't let the phrase become a compliment. If every human bears the image of the Maker, dignity isn't something a culture grants and can take away; it's given at the source. Help the room see how much rests on it, from how we treat the poor to how we treat ourselves. You don't need to settle the theology.

discussion.q: Some people hold that the universe is just matter and energy and that meaning is something we invent. What's strong in that view, and what does it struggle to account for?
discussion.behind: There may be a skeptic in the room, so be fair. The materialist account isn't stupid; it's rigorous and often more careful than lazy faith. Grant that. Then name what it keeps assuming and can't ground: that beauty is real and cruelty is wrong. You're not trying to win, only to make the assumption visible.

discussion.q: The Hebrew word shalom means more than the absence of conflict: everything in its right place. Where have you had a taste of that, and where do you feel its absence most?
discussion.behind: Shalom isn't an abstraction; it's what everyone aches for. Let people name a taste of it, a table, a reconciliation, a morning, and name the absence too. The Bible is describing the thing their own hearts keep reaching for.

discussion.q: If the world is a gift, the natural response is thanks. Where do you live as though what you have were owed to you rather than given?
discussion.behind: Go first. Most of us, leaders included, live with a quiet sense of entitlement and only notice the gift when something is taken away. Help people name specific things: health, food, people, the day itself. This isn't guilt for its own sake; it's the recovery of wonder.

objections.objection: Genesis is a primitive creation myth written by people who didn't know where rain comes from. Science has explained the origin of the universe and of life, so the opening of the Bible is a beautiful story we've outgrown.
objections.response: Grant a good deal of that. Genesis isn't a laboratory report and was never trying to be one, and reading it as a rival to physics or biology misunderstands what kind of writing it is. The people who wrote it didn't have modern meteorology, and modern science is a real achievement worth celebrating. But the objection answers a question Genesis isn't asking. Science can describe the processes by which the universe came to be. It can't tell you why there's something rather than nothing, or why that something is intelligible at all. Genesis is answering that second kind of question: what the world is, and who stands behind it. Its claim, that the world is a gift and not an accident, can't be confirmed or refuted by measurement, because measuring assumes a world that makes sense.

objections.objection: Calling the world "very good" is easy in a garden. It's an insult to anyone standing in a cancer ward or a war zone. A world this full of suffering can't honestly be called very good.
objections.response: Don't rush past this. The person raising it may be raising it from inside a loss. The world as we meet it isn't very good. It's full of suffering that shouldn't be, and any faith that chirps otherwise is lying. But notice the order of the story, because it's the point. Genesis calls the world very good before the fall, not after. The Bible agrees with the objector that the present world isn't as it should be. Suffering is real, and it's an intrusion, a wound in something that was made whole, not part of the original design. That's why the Bible can grieve suffering as a violation instead of shrugging at it as normal. The story doesn't begin by calling the cancer ward good. It begins by insisting the cancer ward isn't how things were meant to be, and it doesn't end until that ward is empty.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: If you really believed the world was a gift and you an image bearer in it, what's one thing you've been treating as owed that you'd start receiving as given?
sessions.practice: This week, once a day, name one thing about the created world as a gift rather than a fact: the taste of coffee, a child's face, the fact that your eyes turn light into sight. Say it out loud or write it down. Don't make it a technique. Let one moment a day be received instead of used. At the end of the week, write down what you saw on the day it was hardest to be grateful.
sessions.closingPrayer: Maker of heaven and earth, before anything was, you were, and you spoke, and the world came to be, and you called it good because you meant it. We've lived in your gift as though we made it. We've used what we were given and thanked no one, and we've treated the image you placed on every face as something that could be earned or erased. Forgive our entitlement and our blindness. Teach us to see the world again as the good thing you made and still love. Give us back the wonder we traded for control, and the thanks we owe you for everything we have. And where the goodness has been broken, hold us until you make it good again. Amen.
reflection: Have I been reading my life as an accident to put up with or as a gift to receive? How would the second change an ordinary Tuesday?
If every person I meet bears the image of God, whom am I treating as less than that, and why?
Where has entitlement replaced gratitude in me so quietly that I've stopped noticing the world was ever a gift?
sessions.teaching:
The quickest way to misread the whole Bible is to open it to the wrong page, and the page most of us open it to is chapter three, the fall. Start there and the human condition becomes the baseline, and grace becomes a ladder out of a hole we assume we were always in. But the story doesn't begin in a hole. It begins in a garden. Before there's any sin to be rescued from, there are six days and a verdict, and the verdict is good. It's spoken six times, and then over the whole of it: "And God saw everything that he had made, and behold, it was very good" (Genesis 1:31).

Where you start decides what you think the story is about. Start at the fall and the Bible is a rescue operation. Start at creation and it's a homecoming, the recovery of something real that was lost, which is a larger thing.

Now, the fight everyone wants to have is about how the world was made, six days or billions of years. I'm not going to have that fight tonight, because Genesis isn't having it either. It isn't trying to beat modern cosmology at its own game. It's answering a question science can't reach: not how the world came to be but what the world is. And its answer is so large that familiarity has made us deaf to it. The world isn't an accident, and it isn't a machine; it's a gift. "In the beginning, God created the heavens and the earth" (Genesis 1:1). Everything that exists is made and dependent, and God alone is not. Reality carries a purpose it didn't give itself.

And the human being, in this account, isn't a clever animal that learned to talk. "So God created man in his own image, in the image of God he created him; male and female he created them" (Genesis 1:27). The human is made from "dust from the ground," with God's own "breath of life" breathed into him (Genesis 2:7): earthy and God-touched at once. He's given work before anything goes wrong, put in the garden "to work it and keep it" (Genesis 2:15). And the first thing God calls not good is loneliness: "It is not good that the man should be alone" (Genesis 2:18). Every intuition you have that a person isn't a thing to be used draws on this page, whether you believe it or not.

Take the strongest case for the other account, because it isn't foolish and the person making it is often more careful than the believer. The materialist story says the universe is matter and energy running down toward cold, that life is chemistry that learned to copy itself, and that meaning is a comforting fiction the brain projects onto a cosmos that doesn't care whether we live or die. Grant its rigor. It has explained more of the world's workings than any account before it. I came to faith from atheism, so I've held this view myself, and most people who hold it do so not out of rebellion but because it seems like the grown-up thing to believe.

But it has to keep assuming the very thing it denies. It can't account for the fact that the world means something. It tells me the sunset is light scattering in the atmosphere, and that's true, and it hasn't touched the thing that makes me stop and call it beautiful. It tells me cruelty is a behavior that once helped my ancestors survive, and I know as surely as I know my own name that cruelty isn't merely unhelpful. It's wrong. The materialist has to live every day as though the world means something while his account says it doesn't. That gap is very hard to close without God.

Here's the word the whole Bible will spend itself trying to recover, so learn it tonight; we'll need it for all five sessions. Shalom. We translate it "peace," but it's bigger than the absence of conflict. It's everything in its right place: the human at peace with God above him, with the neighbor beside him, with the creation in his care, and with his own restless self. That's the world that was good.

And this is where the first act names all of us. We don't live as though the world were a gift. We live as though it were owed to us, and we notice the giving only when something is taken away. Modern life trains us toward that entitlement, and we're well trained. So the first act of the story isn't just information. It's a call back to wonder, back to the posture of a creature who didn't make himself, standing in a world he didn't build, saying the only fitting thing: thank you. Everything the rest of the Bible does is either the story of how we lost that world, or the long, costly work of God to give it back.

scriptureStudy.note: "In the beginning, God created the heavens and the earth." The Bible's first sentence is an announcement, not an argument. Everything that exists is made and dependent, and God alone is the uncreated source. From the first line, the human is a creature, not an owner.

"Then God said, 'Let us make man in our image, after our likeness.' ... So God created man in his own image." Human dignity rests not on usefulness or achievement but on bearing the Maker's image, a status given at creation that no failure erases and no culture can revoke.

"And God saw everything that he had made, and behold, it was very good." The verdict over the whole creation is emphatic. The material world, the body, work and pleasure are gifts, not obstacles to spiritual life, and evil comes later as an intruder.

"Then the Lord God formed the man of dust from the ground and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life, and the man became a living creature." Dust and breath at once: earthy and God-touched, neither angel nor animal.

"The Lord God took the man and put him in the garden of Eden to work it and keep it." Work comes before the fall. It's a calling, not a curse: the human invited to tend and guard a good world under its Maker.
"It is not good that the man should be alone." The first thing called not good is solitude. Human community is written into creation, and the shalom of the garden was always shared.

"The heavens declare the glory of God, and the sky above proclaims his handiwork." Creation isn't mute. It speaks of the one who made it, which is why the sense that a sunset means something may be hearing rather than projecting.

sessions.goingDeeper:
For the group that wants more, look at the distance between the ancient text and the modern reader, because the way we see the world was itself shaped by history. In A Secular Age (2007), the philosopher Charles Taylor described a long shift from an "enchanted" world, where meaning came from outside the self and the world was charged with it, to what he called the buffered self, which treats meaning as something it supplies to neutral matter. Ask the group how much of the modern difficulty with Genesis is about evidence, and how much is this prior shift, which taught us ahead of time that the world is inert stuff and any meaning in it must be ours.

Set that beside the older Jewish and Christian conviction that the world is a sign, spoken by a God who speaks. To read creation as gift isn't to add a religious layer to bare facts. It's to see the facts as they are.

Then test the secular account at its strongest. Critics of religion have been right that a faith which pits Genesis against biology as a rival explanation of mechanism deserves to lose, and Christians have done real harm fighting on that ground. But grant that, and a deeper question remains. Ludwig Wittgenstein wrote in his Tractatus (1921) that what is mystical is not how the world is, but that it is. Science works inside existence; it can't get behind it to say why there's a stage for anything to happen on. Genesis and physics are answering different questions, and the question Genesis answers is one no experiment will settle and no thoughtful person can finally avoid.
sessions.caseStudy:
Suppose a man in your group is a scientist, careful and fair-minded. He says quietly that he loves the study, but he can't switch off the part of his mind that knows the universe is nearly fourteen billion years old while Genesis speaks of six days, and he isn't going to check his brain at the door. He isn't hostile; he's naming a real tension.

Honor his integrity before you press anything. Don't ask him to choose between his science and the text, because that's a false choice this study rejects, and pushing it would only confirm his fear that faith requires him to lie to himself. Thank him for refusing to pretend.

Then, gently, help him notice that Genesis and his cosmology may not be competing at all. The text is answering what and who and why; his science answers how. And his own wonder at the order of the universe, the thing that made him a scientist in the first place, may be closer to Genesis than to the flat materialism he thinks he's supposed to hold. You don't need to settle the age of the earth tonight. The aim is to free him to read the opening of the Bible as the kind of writing it is, with his brain fully engaged. Then ask the group whether any of them have felt that same pull between what they know and what they read.

sessions.title: The Fall, and the Unraveling of Everything
sessions.aim: To read Genesis 3 as the diagnosis of what's wrong with the world and with us: the good creation broken at every level, sin understood as the ruin of shalom rather than mere rule-breaking, and the human condition named plainly before any rescue is offered.
sessions.summary:
The fall may be the one Christian teaching that hardly needs arguing, only pointing at. Every newspaper is evidence for it, and so is every truthful look in the mirror. The real question isn't whether the world is broken but what broke it. Genesis 3 answers that the break is moral and spiritual, a rupture between the creature and his Maker that cracked outward into everything else.

The serpent's lie isn't crude. It's that God is holding out on you, and that the way to become fully yourself is to take the right to define good and evil for yourself. Some argue that sin is a concept invented to control people through guilt. The church has abused guilt, and that should be admitted plainly. But we don't need an institution to give us the weight of a wrong we know we did.

The fall breaks four relationships at once: with God, with ourselves in shame, with our neighbor in blame, and with creation in thorns and toil. It isn't only what happened to other people long ago. It happens in each of us. And on the same page, God makes the first promise of rescue.

keyScripture.why: "For God knows that when you eat of it your eyes will be opened, and you will be like God, knowing good and evil" (Genesis 3:5). The heart of the fall isn't a broken rule but the creature taking the right to decide good and evil for himself. That's the lie under every sin since.

discussion.q: Where do you see evidence that something has gone wrong with the world, and where do you see it in yourself?
discussion.behind: Start on shared ground; almost no one denies the world is broken. Then move gently from the world out there to the self in here. The fall is most persuasive not in the headlines but in each person's memory of something they did that they can't fully explain. Keep it truthful, not morbid.

discussion.q: Read Genesis 3:1-6. The serpent suggests God is holding out on them. Where does that same suggestion show up in your life now?
discussion.behind: Make the old temptation present. It isn't about fruit; it's about who gets to decide what's good. Help the room hear its modern form: the sense that nobody, God included, gets to tell me what's right for me. Don't moralize; let people recognize the voice.

discussion.q: Some people say sin is a concept invented to control people through guilt. What's true in that, and where does it break down?
discussion.behind: The church has used guilt as a weapon, and anger at that is earned, so grant it fully. Then ask whether the idea can really be dismissed, since a person who has done real wrong doesn't need an institution to invent the weight they already feel. Separate the abuse of the word from the reality it names.

discussion.q: Read Genesis 3:7-19. The fall breaks things between people and God, within themselves, between each other, and with the ground. Which of those four breaks do you feel most right now?
discussion.behind: This is the center of the evening. Some feel distance from God, some shame in the mirror, some a broken relationship, some the frustration of work and a failing body. Let people locate themselves. The rescue will have to reach all four.

discussion.q: Adam reaches, hides and then blames the woman and God (Genesis 3:12). Where have you seen that pattern of reaching, hiding and blaming in yourself this week?
discussion.behind: Go first, and keep it brief and real. This isn't meant to crush anyone. Grace means little until the ruin is named, and the leader's candor gives the room permission. If someone's wound is deeper than the evening can hold, offer to talk afterward.

objections.objection: Sin is a made-up concept, a tool religion invented to make people feel guilty and afraid so the church could sell them the cure. Get rid of the guilt and people are basically good and doing their best.
objections.response: Grant the accusation where it's earned, and it's earned more than believers like to admit. The church has used guilt as a lever and manufactured shame to control people, and anger at that manipulation is closer to justice than to sin. Say so without hedging. But look at what the objection assumes, that people are basically good and doing their best, and set that next to the record, not of monsters far away but of ourselves. Most of us carry the memory of something we did that nobody forced, that helped no one, that we knew was wrong while we did it. No church installed that weight. It was already there, which is exactly why the guilt lever worked. The word sin doesn't invent the weight. It takes it seriously enough to do something about it other than tell you to stop feeling it. Being told you're basically fine isn't freedom. It's being told your wound is imaginary by someone with no bandage.

objections.objection: Blaming everything on a couple eating fruit in a garden is childish. Human problems have real causes: poverty, trauma, unjust systems, poor education. Calling it all sin lets people off the hook for fixing the actual conditions.
objections.response: This is pointing at something the church has too often ignored. Suffering does have near causes. Poverty, trauma and unjust systems are real and must be fought, and a piety that spiritualizes every wound while ignoring what produced it is condemned by Scripture itself; read Amos. Grant all of that. But the objection pushes the cause back one step and then stops. The next question can't be avoided: why are systems unjust? Why do the strong exploit the weak? Why is trauma so often passed down instead of healed? Every social cause runs back into human hearts that chose it. The fall isn't a rival to those causes; it describes the soil they grow in. Naming sin doesn't excuse anyone from fixing conditions. It refuses the shallower hope that if we fixed the conditions the human heart would come out clean, a hope the twentieth century tested at terrible cost.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: What's one thing you did that no one made you do, that you've spent real energy explaining away? What would it mean to call it what it is?
sessions.practice: This week, catch yourself once in the oldest move in the story: the blame shift, the reflex to make your wrong someone else's fault. Don't announce it. Notice it, and then do the harder thing: name your part plainly, to yourself and to God, and if it fits, to the person involved. At the end of the week, write down what happened in you when you stopped hiding, and whether being in the open was as unbearable as hiding had promised.
sessions.closingPrayer: Lord God, you made a good world and put it in our hands, and we listened to the voice that said you were holding out on us. We reached for what wasn't ours, the right to be our own gods and decide good and evil for ourselves. And it broke: our peace with you, with each other, with the ground and with our own hearts. We've been hiding ever since, covering ourselves and blaming the person beside us, and blaming you for giving them. We aren't basically fine. We've done things no one made us do, and we know it. Don't let us explain them away. Meet us in the open as you met the first ones, not with the ruin we deserved but with a promise we didn't, and hold us until the story you began that day is finished. Amen.
reflection: Where am I still believing the serpent's suggestion that God is holding out on me, and that any limit he sets is an attack on my freedom?
Which of the four breaks, with God, with myself, with a neighbor or with the world, am I most tempted to pretend isn't really broken?
What's my version of hiding among the trees, the way I cover what I've done instead of bringing it into the open?
sessions.teaching:
There's one Christian doctrine you hardly ever have to argue for, only point at, and it's this one. You can debate the resurrection, the Trinity and the authority of Scripture, and thoughtful people will line up on both sides. But the claim that something has gone deeply and universally wrong with human beings and the world they live in barely needs defending. The evidence is in every newspaper and in every quiet hour we've spent alone with our own memories. So we come to Genesis 3, and we have to read it without flinching, because a rescue that won't first name the ruin isn't good news. It's sentiment with a verse attached.

The real question isn't whether the world is broken. Almost nobody denies that. The question is what broke it. Most modern answers locate the break somewhere manageable: in our economics, our politics, our institutions, our lack of education, somewhere out there that the right program could fix. Genesis locates it somewhere more serious. It puts the break in the relationship between the creature and his Maker, and from there it cracks outward into everything else.

Notice how it happens: the serpent's approach isn't crude. He opens with a question: "Did God actually say, 'You shall not eat of any tree in the garden'?" (Genesis 3:1). Then he makes his offer: "For God knows that when you eat of it your eyes will be opened, and you will be like God, knowing good and evil" (Genesis 3:5). He doesn't say disobey for fun. He says God is holding out on you. The limit isn't love; it's envy. The way to become fully yourself is to take the authority to decide good and evil on your own terms.

And they took it. "She took of its fruit and ate, and she also gave some to her husband who was with her, and he ate" (Genesis 3:6). We still take it, every day, because this isn't only an ancient temptation. It's close to the founding creed of the modern self: that nobody, not even the God who made me, gets to tell me what's good, and that any limit is a kind of oppression.

Take the strong case against all this, because the person making it has often been wounded by the church. It says sin is a concept religion invented to make people afraid, so the institution could sell the cure for a disease it made up. I have to grant, without hedging, that the church has used guilt as a lever and produced shame to control people. The anger at that is right.

But look at what the objection has to assume: that underneath it all people are basically good and doing their best. Set that next to the evidence, which isn't the monster on the news but the face in the mirror. You know the thing you did that nobody made you do, that helped no one, that you knew was wrong while you did it. Nobody had to install that weight in you. It was already there, which is why the guilt lever worked at all. The word sin doesn't invent the weight. It's a diagnosis serious enough to take the weight seriously.

Now look at how far the break runs, because it isn't one break. It's four, and they open at once. First, the man and woman are cut off from God: they "hid themselves from the presence of the Lord God among the trees of the garden" (Genesis 3:8). Second, they're cut off from themselves: "the eyes of both were opened, and they knew that they were naked" (Genesis 3:7), and they cover themselves in shame. Third, they're cut off from each other. Watch how quickly it happens: "The woman whom you gave to be with me, she gave me fruit of the tree, and I ate" (Genesis 3:12). The man blames the woman and God in a single breath. Fourth, they're cut off from the creation. The ground is cursed, work turns to sweat and thorns, and the body turns toward dust (Genesis 3:17-19). Four relationships, all good in the garden, all broken in an afternoon, and every one is a wound the rest of the Bible will have to heal.

I can't tell this as other people's problem, because it isn't. The fall happens in each of us, me included. We make the same reach to be the one who decides what's good for us. We do the same hiding afterward, arranging the version of ourselves that doesn't need forgiving. And we do the same blaming, the reflex to make our wrong somebody else's fault, and if nobody's handy, God's. That's the bottom of the story, and we won't rush past it, because everything good that's coming depends on our being willing to stand for one evening in the truth that we aren't basically fine.

Paul read this chapter as the hinge of human history: "sin came into the world through one man, and death through sin, and so death spread to all men because all sinned" (Romans 5:12). We're east of Eden, all of us, and we can't get back in on our own. But the same chapter that shuts the gate holds the first whisper that God isn't finished. Speaking to the serpent, God says of the woman's offspring, "he shall bruise your head, and you shall bruise his heel" (Genesis 3:15). The ruin is total. And already, on the same page, grace has started to move.

scriptureStudy.note: "Did God actually say, 'You shall not eat of any tree in the garden'?" The serpent's first move is a question that makes God's word sound doubtful and his limit arbitrary. Doubt about God's goodness comes before the disobedience.

"She took of its fruit and ate, and she also gave some to her husband who was with her, and he ate." The act is small and the cost is enormous, which is how sin works. And the man was there with her, silent.

"Then the eyes of both were opened, and they knew that they were naked." The first result of taking autonomy isn't godlike freedom but shame: exposure where there had been safety. It's the opposite of what the serpent promised.
"The man and his wife hid themselves from the presence of the Lord God among the trees of the garden." After sin, the reflex is to hide from the one who could heal it.

"The woman whom you gave to be with me, she gave me fruit of the tree, and I ate." The man blames the woman and God together, the woman blames the serpent (verse 13), and the first human community breaks into accusation.

"He shall bruise your head, and you shall bruise his heel." Inside the curse is the first promise of rescue: an offspring of the woman will one day crush the serpent. Grace begins on the same page as the ruin.

"Sin came into the world through one man, and death through sin, and so death spread to all men because all sinned." Paul reads Genesis 3 not as a tale about two people but as the account of a condition that reaches everyone, the ruin Christ comes to reverse.

sessions.goingDeeper:
For the group that wants more, look at our discomfort with the very word sin, because that discomfort has a history. In The Triumph of the Therapeutic (1966), the sociologist Philip Rieff described the slow replacement of a moral culture, where the self is measured against a standard outside it, by a therapeutic one, where the highest goal is well-being and guilt is a symptom to manage rather than a signal to heed. Ask the group how much of the difficulty with the fall is intellectual and how much is cultural, the water of an age that has taught us in advance that talk of sin is unhealthy.

Set that beside the older Christian claim that naming sin truthfully isn't the enemy of health but a condition of real freedom, because a wound can't be healed while it's being called something else. And notice that Scripture never confuses sin with the wounds others inflict on us. Being sinned against is not the same as sinning.

Then take the secular accounts of human brokenness at their strongest. Students of trauma and of social conditioning have often been right about how people are shaped and harmed. Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn, who spent eight years in Soviet prison camps and had every reason to blame the system, wrote in The Gulag Archipelago that the line dividing good and evil runs not between states or classes or parties but through every human heart. Grant what the therapeutic and social accounts see truly. Then press the question they struggle to answer: why the line runs through the heart of the victim as well as the victimizer. That's what Genesis 3 has been saying all along.
sessions.caseStudy:
Suppose a woman in your group grew up in a harsh church where sin was preached as a club and she was made to feel worthless from childhood. She flinches every time the word comes up. She tells the group she's spent years in counseling learning that she isn't the terrible person she was told she was. She isn't being difficult. She's carrying a real wound the church gave her.

Honor her healing before you add any weight. Don't correct her, and don't suggest that her hard-won sense of her own worth is the pride this session is talking about; that would reopen the wound. Say plainly that what was done to her was itself a sin against her, a misuse of the very doctrine we're studying, and that the God of this story never called her worthless. Genesis 1 called her an image bearer before Genesis 3 ever happened.

Then, if there's trust and room, help her see a difference. The shame that was put on her is a lie about who she is, and the gospel comes to take it away. The plain naming of particular wrongs any of us have done is something else, and the gospel comes to forgive it. A sin named can be forgiven; a sin denied can only be carried. The aim isn't to make her feel worse. It's to help her set down a false weight she was never meant to carry. Offer to talk with her privately, and if the old wounds are heavy, help her find a counselor or pastor she can trust; Find Help on the site is a place to start.

sessions.title: Israel, and the Long Faithfulness of God
sessions.aim: To read the Old Testament after Eden, from Abraham through the Exodus and David to the prophets and the long silence, as the unfolding of one promise through one covenant people rather than a set of disconnected hero stories, so that the reader sees why the story needed so many centuries and so much waiting before the turning came.
sessions.summary:
Many people give up on the Old Testament because they were handed it as a pile of unrelated Sunday school stories, Noah and the ark, David and Goliath, Daniel and the lions, with no thread between them. A pile with no thread really is as confusing as it seems.

The thread is a single promise God makes to a childless old man: "in you all the families of the earth shall be blessed" (Genesis 12:3). Everything from Genesis 12 to the end of the Old Testament works that promise out against every obstacle, including the repeated failures of the people who carry it. The Exodus makes a people. David narrows the promise to a king. The prophets call a faithless people back and promise a faithfulness God will one day supply himself.

The strongest objection is that the God of the Old Testament is violent and cruel. Some of the texts are hard, and they shouldn't be waved away. But read whole, the dominant note is God's patience with a people who keep breaking faith. And the Old Testament doesn't end resolved. It ends with a people back in their land, still under empire, and roughly four hundred years without a prophet. God was teaching them to wait.

keyScripture.why: "I will make of you a great nation, and I will bless you ... and in you all the families of the earth shall be blessed" (Genesis 12:2-3). This one promise to Abraham is the thread through the whole Old Testament. Every later story is a chapter in its keeping.

discussion.q: How were you first taught the Old Testament stories? Did they feel connected to each other, and what might change if you read them as one promise being kept?
discussion.behind: Most people carry the Old Testament as a jumble of episodes, morally confusing and seemingly random. Hearing that it's one story is genuinely new to many. Don't defend the hard parts yet. Just reframe the shape from a pile of stories to a single arc.

discussion.q: Read Genesis 12:1-3. God's plan hangs on one promise to one old, childless man. Why do you think God chose to work through one small, failing people rather than fixing everything at once?
discussion.behind: Sit with the strangeness of the method. God doesn't wave the world clean; he starts a family. The slowness isn't a flaw. He's making a people, not just solving a problem. Ask what that suggests about how God still works, slowly and through particular people.

discussion.q: What in the Old Testament troubles you most? Where might reading one passage on its own, cut off from the larger story, distort it?
discussion.behind: The skeptic's objection here is often sincere and sometimes comes from careful reading. Don't paper over the hard texts. Let people say what disturbs them. Then ask whether reading each episode in isolation, away from the covenant and the arc, might mislead. Aim for candor about the difficulty, not a quick defense.

discussion.q: The prophets kept calling a faithless people back and kept being ignored. Where do you hear a call to come back, and where are you, like Israel, not coming?
discussion.behind: Make the prophets personal rather than historical. Everyone has their own version of a call they keep not answering. Go first if the room is slow. This is the prophets turned toward us, not a lecture about ancient Israel.

discussion.q: The Old Testament ends with centuries of waiting and no prophet. What's it like for you to wait on God, and what does Israel's long wait suggest about how God keeps a promise?
discussion.behind: This is the pastoral heart of the session. About two thousand years passed from Abraham to Jesus, and the last four hundred or so had no prophet. Let people be truthful about how hard waiting is. Let Israel's story suggest that silence isn't the same as absence. End with weight: a promise not yet kept, but never abandoned.

objections.objection: The God of the Old Testament is a moral monster: jealous, violent, obsessed with rules and blood, ordering the slaughter of whole peoples. No decent person could worship him, and his critics have been right to say so.
objections.response: Don't flinch from the hardest texts. Pretending they're easy insults a careful reader, and some of these passages should trouble anyone paying attention. The conquest stories and the judgment texts are genuinely difficult, Christians have often used them badly, and a faith that waves them away hasn't read them. Concede that. But the objection reads the story flat. It lifts each episode out of the arc that gives it meaning and out of the ancient world it was spoken into, then judges a long story by its hardest fragment. Read whole, it's the record of a God who binds himself again and again to a people who break faith with him, and who refuses to destroy them when the terms of the covenant said he could. He describes himself as "merciful and gracious, slow to anger, and abounding in steadfast love and faithfulness" (Exodus 34:6), and the story bears that out far more often than it doesn't. The hard texts have to be read inside that portrait. That doesn't make them easy. It does mean the portrait the objection paints isn't the whole one.

objections.objection: Even if there's a story, it's a tribal story: one small people claiming their local god is everyone's God. That's ancient nationalism, the same thing every empire does when it calls its own tribe the chosen ones.
objections.response: That suspicion is watching for something real and dangerous, the drafting of God into a tribe. Israel was tempted to it, and the church has done it again and again. Religious nationalism is idolatry wherever it shows up. But look at what the promise to Abraham actually says, because it runs the other way. It isn't that Abraham's people will rule all the families of the earth, but that through them all the families of the earth will be blessed. They're chosen for service, not privilege, to carry a blessing meant for everyone, including the nations Israel feared. And the prophets condemn Israel more harshly than they condemn anyone else. Amos lists the sins of the nations around Israel and then turns his sharpest words on Israel itself (Amos 1 to 2). A tribal story flatters the tribe. This one indicts it and points past it to a blessing for the whole world.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: Where are you in a long season of waiting on something that hasn't come? What would it mean to read Israel's centuries of waiting as evidence that God is faithful rather than absent?
sessions.practice: This week, read one of the psalms of lament slowly, Psalm 13 or Psalm 22 or Psalm 88, and let it give you words for a place where you're waiting or hurting. Don't tidy it up. Israel prayed its waiting truthfully, and God kept those prayers in the book. Then notice one place this week where you're being called back, as the prophets called Israel, and take one step toward turning. Write down what it was like to pray your waiting in words God already provided.
sessions.closingPrayer: Faithful God, you spoke one promise to one old man and kept it across centuries and countless betrayals, and you never let it die. You made a people and bore with them. You sent them prophets they ignored and mercy they refused, and still you didn't walk away. We're that people. We break faith before breakfast, and you keep faith across generations. Teach us your long patience. Teach us to wait as Israel waited, not as people who think you've forgotten but as people who trust you're at work in the silence. And where we've made you into a god for our own side, forgive us, and remind us we were blessed to be a blessing to every family on earth. Amen.
reflection: Have I read the Old Testament as a jumble of stories? What would it mean to read it as God's long faithfulness to an unfaithful people, including me?
Where have I quietly decided God has forgotten a promise, when Israel's long waiting suggests he may be working in the silence?
Where have I made God the god of my tribe or my side, when the covenant was a blessing meant to run through me to everyone?
sessions.teaching:
Almost everyone who gives up on the Old Testament gives up for the same reason. They were handed it as a pile of unconnected stories, Noah and the flood, Abraham and the knife, Joseph and the coat, Moses and the sea, David and the giant, Daniel and the lions, each taught on its own, with no thread running through them. A pile of stories with no thread really is as baffling as it seemed when you quit. Half of them are violent and strange, the other half seem to come down to "be brave like this person," and without the thread there's no reason to keep reading. So tonight is about the thread, because once you see it, the pile becomes a story.

The thread begins with a single promise to a childless old man from Ur, a man named Abram who had done nothing to deserve it. "Go from your country and your kindred and your father's house to the land that I will show you. And I will make of you a great nation, and I will bless you and make your name great, so that you will be a blessing. I will bless those who bless you, and him who dishonors you I will curse, and in you all the families of the earth shall be blessed" (Genesis 12:1-3). That's the thread. From Genesis 12 to the end of the Old Testament, the whole story works out that promise against every obstacle that rises to stop it, including the biggest one: the repeated failure of the people chosen to carry it. And notice how it starts. "He believed the Lord, and he counted it to him as righteousness" (Genesis 15:6). From the beginning, the promise is received by trust.

Follow the thread and the pile organizes itself. In the Exodus, God makes a people, buying a nation of slaves out of Egypt. "I have surely seen the affliction of my people who are in Egypt and have heard their cry ... and I have come down to deliver them" (Exodus 3:7-8). At Sinai he binds himself to them and gives them a calling: "you shall be to me a kingdom of priests and a holy nation" (Exodus 19:6). Priests stand between God and others, so the whole nation is meant to carry God's blessing outward.

With David, the promise narrows to a king and a throne. God says of David's son, "I will establish the throne of his kingdom forever" (2 Samuel 7:13). And the prophets are the covenant's conscience. When the people break the covenant, God sends them to call the people back, to warn them, and finally, when they won't come, to promise something astonishing: that God himself will supply the faithfulness they can't. "I will put my law within them, and I will write it on their hearts. And I will be their God, and they shall be my people" (Jeremiah 31:33). Isaiah describes a servant who suffers for others: "he was pierced for our transgressions; he was crushed for our iniquities" (Isaiah 53:5). It's one story. It was always one story.

Take the strongest case for the other reading, because it's often made sincerely. It says the God of the Old Testament is a moral monster: jealous, violent, demanding blood, unworthy of any decent person's worship. I'm not going to pretend the hard texts are easy. The conquest narratives are difficult, and the judgment texts are difficult. Grant that its full weight.

But see what the objection does. It reads the story flat. It lifts a single dark episode out of a long arc, cuts it from the covenant that gives it meaning and from the ancient world it was spoken into, and judges the whole by the fragment, which is the reading-in-pieces mistake we started with. Read whole, the dominant note isn't slaughter. It's patience. God binds himself again and again to a people who break faith with him, and he refuses to destroy them when the covenant gave him the right. The real shock of the Old Testament isn't that God judges. It's how long he doesn't, how many times Israel earns the end and receives instead another prophet, another rescue, another chance.

And here we have to stop narrating Israel and admit that we're Israel. The prophets aren't only preaching to people far away. We hear the call to come back, and we don't come. We know the drift: the security we trust more than God, the comfort we serve, the self we keep putting first. We hear the word calling us home, count the cost, and stay where we are, as Israel did, generation after generation. The Old Testament is a mirror, and the face in it is ours.

And then the way it ends, which is that it doesn't. After the patriarchs, the Exodus, the kings, the prophets, the exile and the return, the Old Testament closes with a people back in their land but still under foreign empire, still waiting. Then come roughly four hundred years with no prophet, the promise to Abraham now some two thousand years old and still not fully kept. Many of us know that silence: the prayer that seems to get no answer, the promise you watch the years go by on. Israel sat in it for centuries. What the story quietly teaches is that silence isn't absence. Paul would later say that Christ came "when the fullness of time had come" (Galatians 4:4). The Old Testament ends unresolved on purpose. It ends leaning forward, a promise kept in part and pointing past itself, and a people taught by long experience of God's faithfulness to do the thing we find hardest. Wait.

scriptureStudy.note: "Go from your country ... to the land that I will show you. ... and in you all the families of the earth shall be blessed." The founding promise of the story. Israel is chosen not for privilege but to carry a blessing to the whole world.

"And he believed the Lord, and he counted it to him as righteousness." Abraham is counted righteous by trusting God's promise, centuries before the law. Paul will build on this (Romans 4): the covenant was about trust from the start.

"I have surely seen the affliction of my people ... and have heard their cry ... and I have come down to deliver them." God sees, hears and comes down to rescue slaves. The Exodus becomes the pattern for every rescue after it.

"You shall be my treasured possession among all peoples, for all the earth is mine; and you shall be to me a kingdom of priests and a holy nation." At Sinai God binds himself to a people and gives them a vocation: to stand as priests between him and the nations.
"I will establish the throne of his kingdom forever." God narrows the promise to David's line, a king whose throne will not end, planting the hope of a coming son of David.
"I will put my law within them, and I will write it on their hearts." When the people can't keep the covenant, God promises a new one, supplying from his side the faithfulness they lack.

"But he was pierced for our transgressions; he was crushed for our iniquities." Centuries before the cross, the prophet describes a servant who suffers for the sins of many. It's the clearest bridge from Israel's long wait to Christ.

sessions.goingDeeper:
For the group that wants more, consider the Old Testament as a story rather than a code. N. T. Wright has argued, in The New Testament and the People of God (1992), that many Jews in Jesus' day experienced their Scriptures as an unfinished story, a drama waiting for its ending, and asked when and how God would finally act. Ask the group how differently the Old Testament reads as the early acts of a play rather than a rulebook or an anthology, and how much of the modern complaint against it comes from expecting a code and finding a story.

Then take up the hard texts with more time than the session allows. Christians have read the conquest narratives in several ways: as particular judgments in a particular time that aren't a pattern for anyone after; as accounts written in the stylized battle language of the ancient Near East, which often exaggerated for effect; as genuine moral difficulties to be carried honestly rather than solved. Let the group weigh these without settling too fast. And remember the early answer that was rejected: in the second century Marcion tried to cut the Old Testament out altogether, and the church refused, because without it the story of Jesus loses its meaning.

Then the pastoral turn, toward waiting. In a culture of instant everything, we read divine silence as divine absence. The whole Old Testament trains the opposite instinct. Waiting in Scripture isn't passive resignation but active, hoping trust, and the God who kept a promise across two thousand years is not likely to have forgotten the smaller ones we're waiting on now.
sessions.caseStudy:
Suppose a young man in your group is drawn to Jesus but says he can't get past the Old Testament. The violence, the strange laws and a God who seems so different from the one Jesus shows are a wall he can't climb, and he half wishes the church would quietly drop the first two-thirds of the Bible. He's sincere, and his difficulty is an old one. In the second century a teacher named Marcion tried to solve it by cutting the Old Testament out entirely.

Honor his candor before you press. Don't shame the question or rush to defend every hard text; a glib answer would only confirm his suspicion that faith requires him not to look. Tell him Christians have wrestled with this for two thousand years, and that cutting the Old Testament out was tried early and rejected, because without it the story of Jesus has no meaning: a rescue with no account of what we're rescued from and no promise being kept.

Then help him see that the God he's drawn to in Jesus, the God who sees the afflicted and comes down and binds himself to people who don't deserve it, is on page after page of the Old Testament once it's read as one story. The aim isn't to make him pretend the hard texts are easy. It's to show him that the same God has been keeping one promise, patiently, the whole way through. Then ask the group which Old Testament story has been hardest for them, and read it together in its place in the larger arc.
